storm.summary_layperson: Scattered strong storm cells are rotating through the wider region this evening, with one tracked to pass near the cove around 6:30 PM; the Sound is unusually warm right now so it won't offer its usual cooling protection against these storms.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Water and air temperatures are almost identical today (75°F vs 75°F), so there's no stabilizing marine layer to weaken storms before they reach the cove.
storm.detail_html:
Radar shows a cluster of showers and thunderstorms across the wider metro area, with several cells reaching 50–60 dBZ within 12–25 miles west and northwest of the cove. Bulk shear is a healthy 24 kt and CAPE sits at 1,320 J/kg — enough instability for organized cells, though below the 1,500 J/kg threshold where storms typically punch through any protective layer regardless of local conditions.

Normally the cool Sound creates a stabilizing marine layer that weakens storms as they cross the water. Not today: water and air temperature are within 0.2°F of each other, so the marine-layer protective mechanism is inactive. That means the cove has no local advantage over inland towns like Stamford or White Plains — whatever reaches the shoreline reaches the water at roughly full strength.

Most of the nearby high-reflectivity cells (11–25 mi out, including a 54 dBZ cell 23 mi WNW) are tracking away from the cove as the broader system races southwest at 52 kt. The one cell still classified as "closing" is farther out — 42 miles NNW — and closing at a comparatively modest 21 kt.

Most likely outcome for the cove: a chance of a passing shower or embedded thunderstorm cell in the 6:00–7:00 PM window, similar to or slightly wetter than what surrounding inland areas see, since there's no Sound-effect cushion tonight. This is a notably different setup than a typical humid summer evening here.

What would change the call: any cell reclassifying from "moving away" to "closing" on the next radar update, or CAPE building past 1,500 J/kg, would push this toward high risk. A weakening trend in the tracked cell's reflectivity or an increase in its distance would support downgrading to low.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 42 mi NNW closing at 21 kt as the broader system races southwest at 52 kt; with no marine layer active tonight, don't count on the Sound to weaken or delay it the way it might on a typical summer evening.

wind.tactics_blurb: No sea breeze today — the air-to-water temperature gap is only 0.2°F, so this is purely a light, wandering gradient flow that nearby storm cells could kick around through early evening. Stay center on the course and play the shifts rather than committing to a side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a light gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day (B-light). The air–water temperature difference is just 0.2°F — far short of the ~5°F needed to drive a thermal sea breeze — and the coastal station ensemble confirms it: only 30% of coastal stations are reading southerly, versus the persistent-southerly majority you'd see on a real thermal day. The synoptic gradient itself is weak, with the authoritative airport-anemometer average at just 7.7 kt.

Direction agreement across the station ensemble is low (0.43, well under the 0.7 threshold that usually signals a clean, trustworthy read), which lines up with what's happening regionally: scattered thunderstorm cells passing 12–40 miles to the west and northwest are disturbing the local flow with outflow-influenced gusts and shifts rather than a clean synoptic direction. RYC is currently reading WNW at 8.5 kt (13.9 kt gusts, 7.6 kt 10-min average) while the wider ensemble median sits at SSW — a large divergence that reflects this local unsettled character rather than a model/obs sea-breeze lag (the maturation correction doesn't apply on a non-thermal day).

Given the directional scatter, no single side of the course holds a clear geography-driven edge tonight — favor the center and expect to play shifts reactively rather than committing early to one shore.

Shift character through the window: expect the most erratic behavior 18:00–19:00 while nearby convection is closest, then a gradual backing from W/WNW toward SW/SSW as the cells clear out and pass south of the region, with speeds easing toward a light, nearly variable flow by 22:00. None of this is sea-breeze oscillation — it's convective disturbance settling into a weak nocturnal gradient.

Data note: HRRR model guidance beyond the first forecast hour (17:00) was unavailable this run — NOMADS had not yet posted f02–f12 for the 20Z cycle at fetch time. The 18:00–22:00 hourly figures above are built from current-observation persistence and the regional storm/gradient trend rather than model output, so treat direction and speed for those hours as lower-confidence, especially through the 18:00–19:00 convective window.
